analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals to meet minimum nurse-to-patient staffing ratios and protects nurses who refuse unsafe assignments.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 98 Democratic cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote, dying in House committees when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every hospital to staff its units with a minimum number of direct-care registered nurses per patient — for example one nurse for every four patients in medical-surgical units and one for every two in intensive care. Hospitals would have to post and record actual staffing for every shift, could not substitute video monitors or mandatory overtime for nurses, and would face federal fines for violations. Nurses could refuse assignments that violate the ratios or that they are not trained for, with protection from retaliation, and Medicare payments to hospitals would be adjusted to cover the added cost.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who would be guaranteed a minimum number of nurses per unit on every shift, and registered and licensed practical nurses, who would get enforceable staffing limits, an end to mandatory overtime for ratio compliance, and legal protection when they refuse an unsafe assignment. Taxpayers who use Medicare would also see hospitals' compliance costs reimbursed through adjusted Medicare payments.

how_it_helps.text: Sets unit-by-unit maximum patient assignments for direct-care registered nurses, such as 1 nurse to 1 patient in trauma and operating rooms, 1 to 2 in intensive care, 1 to 4 in medical-surgical units, and 1 to 6 in well-baby nurseries, with no averaging across shifts or units.

Hospitals must post the actual nurse-to-patient ratio in each unit, keep three years of staffing records open to the public and to nurses' unions, and submit staffing plans to HHS for public inspection.

Nurses may refuse an assignment that violates the ratios or that they are not trained for without being fired, reported to licensing boards, or otherwise retaliated against, and can sue for reinstatement and lost wages.

Hospitals may not impose mandatory overtime to meet the ratios, may not use video monitors in place of an on-site nurse, and face civil penalties of up to $25,000 for a first knowing violation and $50,000 for repeat violations, with violators named publicly by HHS.

Medicare payments to hospitals would be adjusted to cover the net additional costs attributable to complying with the ratios, and the bill adds stipends to nursing scholarship programs and expands nurse retention grants.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals bear the cost of hiring enough nurses to meet fixed ratios on every shift, posting notices, keeping records, and potential fines. Because the bill adjusts Medicare payments to cover compliance costs, part of the bill ultimately falls on the federal Medicare program and taxpayers. Rural hospitals get four years instead of two to comply, an acknowledgment that fixed ratios are harder for smaller facilities to meet.

drawbacks.text: Fixed numeric ratios leave hospitals little flexibility for unusual shifts, and hospitals would need to hire large numbers of additional registered nurses during an existing national nursing shortage — a bill the sponsors' own text acknowledges would need a federal report on 'ensuring that sufficient numbers of nurses are available.'

The Medicare payment adjustment means the public picks up much of the compliance cost through the Medicare program, so savings claimed from better patient outcomes are not guaranteed to offset the added federal spending.
Compliance costs fall hardest on rural and financially struggling hospitals, which get a longer phase-in (four years instead of two) precisely because the requirements are harder for them to meet.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The evidence cited in the bill's own findings — including studies of California's ratio law — links better nurse staffing to better patient outcomes and nurse retention, and the whistleblower protections directly address a documented hospital practice of pressuring nurses into unsafe assignments. The serious costs are real but manageable on their face: hospitals lose staffing flexibility, a nursing shortage makes hiring hard, and Medicare picks up much of the tab. The bill was designed with offsets — Medicare payment adjustments, rural phase-ins, emergency exemptions, and state rules left in place if stricter — which makes the case that its benefits outweigh its costs reasonably strong, though the added federal spending is not fully answered by the outcome studies it cites.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to an Energy and Commerce health subcommittee, and it sat there — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 and the bill expired.

narrative.text: Representative Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on April 6, 2023, with a long initial list of Democratic cosponsors.
It was referred that day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee, splitting its fate between two committees.
On April 14, 2023, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where subcommittee referral is typically the step before — or instead of — a hearing.
The only later action in the entire two-year Congress was a second referral to the same subcommittee on December 17, 2024, weeks before the Congress ended.
The bill ended the Congress with 98 cosponsors, all Democrats, none of whom were on the committees that controlled its schedule.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals are better off because the bill died: they avoided a federal mandate to hire more nurses per unit, publish shift-by-shift staffing records, and pay fines up to $50,000 per knowing violation. Nurses and hospital patients gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals that avoided the staffing mandate

sides.party_line_note: All 98 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-led committees never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would force hospitals to hire more direct-care registered nurses per unit on every shift, ban averaging and mandatory overtime, open their staffing records to public inspection, and expose them to federal fines and public naming for violations. Industry opposition rests on cost and inflexibility, but the mandate directly targets the practice of running understaffed units to save money.

Hospitals needing to meet ratios would likely buy more temporary nurses, raising demand for agencies. The bill conditions this by requiring agency nurses to prove unit competence and receive orientation before assignment.

The bill adds stipends to the federal nursing scholarship program and expands nurse retention grants to preceptorship and mentorship projects, channeling federal money into recruiting and keeping nurses.
